concept.name: Pip
concept.definition: The conventional smallest whole-unit increment of an FX exchange rate quote. For most major currency pairs (priced to four decimal places) one pip is one unit of the fourth decimal place (0.0001); for yen pairs one pip is one unit of the second decimal place (0.01).
concept.intuition: A pip is the FX market's standard 'cent' for talking about exchange-rate moves and spreads.
concept.mechanics: Price changes, bid-ask spreads and forward points are quoted in pips. The monetary value of a pip in quote-currency terms equals the pip size multiplied by the position size in base-currency units; a pip is distinct from the tick size, which in a given market may be a fraction (e.g. 1/2 pip) or multiple of a pip.
concept.formula: Pip value (quote currency) = pip size x position size (base units); pip size = 0.0001 for most pairs, 0.01 for JPY pairs.
concept.failure_modes: The four-decimal convention breaks down for pairs quoted with more or fewer decimals (e.g. JPY pairs at 0.01, or pairs priced to five decimals), so 'pip' must be re-anchored per pair; confusing pips with basis points or ticks misstates spread and P&L figures.
concept.misconceptions: A pip is not a universal 0.01% move in the exchange rate — its percentage value varies with the level of the rate and the pair's decimal convention.
concept.example: If EUR/USD moves from 1.3000 to 1.3010, the pair has risen 10 pips; on a 500,000 EUR position that move is worth 500,000 x 0.0010 = USD 500.
